events.summary: On Thursday, after what it called a 'detailed, 48-hour investigation', ASOS said an 'unauthorised party gained access to an Asos employee account by impersonating a trusted contact to obtain login credentials', then used them to reach 'third-party platforms used by Asos'. Names, addresses, phone numbers, email addresses and customers' search histories were accessed. Payment card details and passwords were not. 'The affected platforms were immediately locked down.' PA's report (Irish Examiner) is timestamped 14:32 Irish time, which is 09:32 New York time, so it came out by about the US open at the latest. Bloomberg's report the same day said the hackers had claimed to compromise ASOS's Snowflake system and that a Snowflake spokesperson later said its platform had not been breached.
events.why_it_matters: This is the first explanation of how the attackers got in, and it points to a tricked ASOS employee rather than a weakness in Snowflake. On Tuesday the hacking claim had cost Snowflake about 2.52 points against software. Snowflake gained 3.17% on Thursday while software (IGV) fell 0.23%, and the gain came during the session (open $332.11, close $343.40). That timing fits the stock recovering Tuesday's loss (inference, medium). ASOS did not name the third-party platforms, so whether data held in ASOS's Snowflake account was reached with the stolen login is still not public.

events.summary: On Friday morning (UK time), Snowflake gave the media a firmer statement than its Tuesday denial: 'We can confirm this issue did not in any way result from a vulnerability, weakness, flaw, or misconfiguration with the Snowflake service', it 'was not caused by Snowflake', and 'No remediation is required for Snowflake customers.' It was a spokesperson's statement to the media, not an SEC filing or a press release on snowflake.com. The Independent's report is timestamped 12:21 CEST (06:21 New York time) and LBC's 11:24 UK time (06:24 New York time).
events.why_it_matters: It removes most of the worry that the 2024 problem was back. In 2024, stolen customer passwords were used to take data from about 165 Snowflake customer accounts. Snowflake's statement is in the same form as its 2024 one: it rules out a flaw in Snowflake's systems, but it does not say whether ASOS's own Snowflake account was opened with the stolen employee login. The stock opened only 0.55% higher on Friday ($345.30 against $343.40) and made most of its gain later in the session, so the statement alone does not explain Friday's 7.4% (inference, medium).

events.summary: Bloomberg reported that OpenAI told investors it expects annualized revenue to reach or exceed $70 billion by the end of 2026, with 77% run-rate growth in its third quarter and 107% in its enterprise business. On Thursday, a Financial Times report that OpenAI's annualized revenue had 'topped out at $50 billion, $20 billion short of estimates' had triggered an AI sell-off (Nasdaq 100 down 1.4%). Bloomberg explained the gap as accounting: OpenAI counts only its own share of sales made through partners, while Anthropic counts the full value of sales through cloud partners. On Friday, tech rebounded: S&P 500 +0.6%, Nasdaq +0.6%, Dow +0.8%. The software fund IGV rose 2.81% and closed at its high for the day ($112.67), and the cybersecurity fund CIBR rose 3.58%. Yahoo Finance's Brian Sozzi described a 'valuation multiple rerating across infrastructure and application software', as fear that AI labs would crush software makers (the 'SaaSpocalypse') faded.
events.why_it_matters: This explains the industry part of Friday's move (+3.09 points). Snowflake tends to move about 1.4 times as much as software on top of the market (model beta), so a strong software day lifts it more than the fund. Faster enterprise AI spending is the demand Snowflake's usage-based model bills for (inference, medium).

why_chain.text: Snowflake rose 3.17% on Thursday and 7.42% on Friday, +10.83% over the two days, to $368.89, 4.07% below its 52-week high of $384.56. The attribution model splits the two days as market +0.17, software +3.36 and company-specific +7.30 (z 1.66). Thursday was almost all company (+3.32); Friday was split between software (+3.09) and company (+3.74).

Thursday: Snowflake rose while software fell 0.23% and AI stocks sold off on the FT's OpenAI revenue report. The gain came during the session (open $332.11, high $344.66, close $343.40, volume 3.99m against 2.47m Wednesday).

Thursday's only Snowflake-specific news found: ASOS said its breach began with an employee tricked into giving up a login (impersonation of a trusted contact) and that 'third-party platforms' were accessed. That points away from a flaw in Snowflake. It was published by about 09:32 New York time.

So Thursday's rise most likely recovered the hacking-claim discount from Tuesday (when the stock lagged software by 2.52 points), now that the findings blamed a human trick at ASOS. No article directly links the stock's rise to this, and no other cause was found (no analyst action, product news or filing).

Friday, part 1 (industry): software rallied 2.81% and closed at its high. Bloomberg reported that OpenAI expects at least $70bn of annualized revenue by year-end, with enterprise run-rate growth of 107%, which reversed Thursday's AI scare. The fear that AI labs would crush software makers keeps fading.

Friday, part 2 (company, +3.74): before the open, Snowflake said the ASOS issue 'was not caused by Snowflake' and 'No remediation is required for Snowflake customers.' But the stock opened only 0.55% higher and climbed through the day to close at its high ($368.89 against a high of $369.04) on 8.0m shares, double its 20-day average. That pattern looks like momentum buying alongside the software rally on top of the cleared trust worry, not a single news shock.

Basic drivers: (a) trust, which is the product for a company that holds customers' data, was restored after a scare; (b) more evidence that companies' AI spending is growing fast, which a usage-billed data platform turns into revenue (37% product revenue growth last quarter); (c) money flowing back into software as the 'AI will kill software' fear fades.

products.name: Snowflake AI Data Cloud: customer accounts ('instances') and their security model
products.what_it_is: Each customer gets its own private account on Snowflake's cloud platform, where it stores data and runs analysis and AI on it.
products.analogy: A safe-deposit box in a bank vault: Snowflake builds and guards the vault, and each customer holds the keys to its own box. If a customer's keys are stolen, its box can be opened without the vault being broken.
products.buyers: Large and mid-size companies (retailers like ASOS, banks, telecoms, software firms) that want one place to store and analyse their data and feed AI tools.
products.how_it_works: Customers' employees and apps log in to their company's account. Snowflake runs the computing that answers their queries and bills for the computing used (consumption, like a taxi meter). Security is split: Snowflake secures the platform, and the customer controls who has logins. Since the 2024 incident, two-step logins are compulsory (per The Register, 2026-10-06, cited in the last report).
products.price: Usage-based (pay per computing credit used); the price per credit varies by edition and region. Not checked in this run: not available.
products.sales: Product revenue $1,491.9 million in Q2 FY2027 (quarter to 2026-07-31), +37% year on year; net revenue retention 126%; Q3 guidance $1,588-1,593 million.
products.size_for_company: This is essentially the whole company: product revenue was about 96% of total revenue of about $1.55 billion last quarter ($1,491.9m / ~$1.55bn, from the thesis numbers table).
products.competition: Databricks, plus the clouds' own data warehouses: Google BigQuery, Amazon Redshift, Microsoft Fabric.
products.why_investors_care: Because billing is by usage, trust and usage are revenue. A real platform breach could slow new workloads; a customer-side login theft is the customer's failure but still revives the 2024 headlines.
products.watch_next: Whether ASOS or investigators say that data in ASOS's Snowflake account was reached with the stolen login; any data leak by the 'Xuanye Group'; Q3 results (about 2026-12-02) for usage trends.
